newsitem.title: UK: Socialist rhetoric, but British Labour's message same.
newsitem.headline: Socialist rhetoric, but British Labour's message same.

text.p: Socialism re-entered the vocabulary of economic policy-makers in Britain's opposition Labour party at its last conference before the election, due in the next seven months.

But behind the attacks on "board-room excesses," speculators and asset-strippers that helped to win shadow finance minister Gordon Brown an ovation on Monday, the message was essentially the same as that Labour has for months been aiming at business leaders.
A Labour government would make macro-economic stability its first priority. There would be no "dash for growth" and no return to penal rates of taxation. The party seeks a partnership with business.

Trade and industry spokeswoman Margaret Beckett, addressing a fringe meeting alongside Confederation of British Industry (CBI) director-general Adair Turner, said there was now much common ground between Labour and the business grouping.
They agreed on the need to improve productivity, invest in skills and develop a high-quality infrastructure.
On key areas of disagreement, such as Labour's plans to introduce a national minimum wage, she acknowledged that "you could introduce a minimum wage and get it wrong."
But, in a reference to the party's determination to be more than a "one-term wonder" in government, she added: "It is not in our interest, any more than yours, to get it wrong."

Alan Milburn, a new recruit to Brown's Treasury team, told another meeting Labour's aim to govern Britain for a generation underpinned its commitment to ending the culture of short-term investment which the party argues has bedevilled the country.
"We want to see a wholesale shift in the investment culture in our country," he said.
Echoing this message, Labour's Treasury spokesman in the House of Lords, John Eatwell, said: "The Labour party in government are going to be investment junkies."
However, Gerald Holtham, head of the left-of-centre Institute for Public Policy Research, warned Labour that it could take a long time to introduce a new investment culture.

He also defended the City of London against charges that it was the main guilty party as far as short-termism is concerned, arguing that most companies had ample access to borrowing but were simply reluctant to "gear up."
Comparing British companies unfavourably with Japan's, Holtham added: "They have a focus on long-term product development. We have a focus on buy and sell."

Brown gave away nothing new on the details of his tax and spending plans. In contrast to his numerous appearances before "City" audiences, he did allow the word "socialism" to cross his lips, but always coupling it with language designed to soothe.
"Our prudence and responsibility is not an abandonment of socialism, it is the very essence of it," he said in his conference speech.

At a fringe meeting on Monday night, the shadow chancellor said he wanted "to re-establish equality as part of the socialist trinity of values" alongside liberty and community. But he quickly made clear he had nothing too radical in mind and was thinking primarily of equality of opportunity.
Brown's keynote speech made almost no reference to European monetary union, which is potentially as much of a minefield for a Labour government as it has been for the Conservatives.
But Eatwell indicated that Labour was sitting on the fence only reluctantly on a single currency.

The party had always taken a generally positive view of monetary union but was alarmed at the "deflationary madness" that had infected continental European governments in their pursuit of "the mystical Maastricht criteria'" Eatwell said.
